title: How harnesses are measured — and how benchmarks mislead
takeaway: A score belongs to a model, harness, task set, and protocol; passing the benchmark is not proof of complete correctness.

scenes.title: A score belongs to a system
scenes.visual: 2.1.1: diagram assembles model, agent harness, task set, and protocol into a score, with no isolated model trophy. 2.1.2: split a SWE-bench board into all-agent and fixed mini-SWE-agent views. 2.1.3: distinguish agent control flow from an outer evaluation-harness boundary; animate a patch through a clean re-grade as an example protocol, not a universal implementation.

sentences.text: A coding-agent score belongs to a model, a harness, a task set, and an evaluation protocol.
SWE-bench separates its all-agent leaderboard from a bash-only model comparison using mini-SWE-agent.
The agent harness does the work; the evaluation harness sets up tasks and grades results.

onScreen.text: Model + agent harness + task set + evaluation protocol = reported system score · SWE-bench all-agent view ≠ fixed mini-SWE-agent model comparison · as of 2026-10-08
Agent harness: prompts, tools, control flow | Evaluation harness: task setup, execution, grading · Pro V2 example: pristine-image patch re-grade

scenes.title: Validity, cost, and held-out evaluation
scenes.visual: 2.5.1: diagram splits false acceptance from false rejection, with source-specific A and C badges. 2.5.2: checklist names task validity, outcome validity, and reporting; keep the historical empty-response example in an inset. 2.5.3: scatter plots only HAL Table A23's GPT-5 Medium pair on cost versus best-run accuracy, with full conditions and no points imported from other tables.

sentences.text: Validity cuts both ways: weak tests accept bad fixes, while overly specific tests or broken environments reject good ones.
The peer-reviewed Agentic Benchmark Checklist separates task validity, outcome validity, and reporting.
AI Agents That Matter recommends cost alongside accuracy and protected holdouts; HAL charts those trade-offs.
sentences.spoken: A I Agents That Matter recommends cost alongside accuracy and protected holdouts; Hal charts those trade offs.

onScreen.text: False acceptance: inadequate tests | False rejection: over-specific tests, unreliable environments · UTBoost research and OpenAI's Verified motivation

scenes.title: Time horizon is task difficulty
scenes.visual: 2.6.1: diagram draws a schematic success curve against human-expert task duration, explicitly labelled illustrative with no fabricated model points. A horizontal selected-success threshold intersects the curve; do not show an agent-runtime stopwatch. 2.6.2: emphasize the clean-task scope caption rather than mapping the curve to workplace hours saved.

sentences.text: METR's time horizon measures task difficulty in human time at a chosen success probability, not agent runtime.
Its clean, self-contained tasks differ from a familiar employee's everyday work.

onScreen.text: METR time horizon · human-expert task duration vs. predicted success · schematic, no model data plotted · not agent runtime; clean self-contained tasks differ from contextual workplace activity
